# 2026 Voter Guide: Florida State Senate, District 6

The following research report provides a comprehensive, nonpartisan analysis of the candidates and dynamics shaping the November 3, 2026, general election for Florida State Senator, District 6. This district encompasses Baker, Bradford, Clay, Columbia, Gilchrist, and Union counties, as well as a portion of Alachua County, bridging rural agricultural areas with suburban and academic centers [1, 2]. The district's boundaries have remained consistent since the 2022 redistricting cycle, which was approved by the Florida Supreme Court in March 2022 [3, 4]. Historically, the political environment of District 6 has leaned heavily conservative, registering an R+28.1 margin in the 2024 presidential election [5]. 

The 2026 contest features three qualified candidates appearing on the general election ballot: Jason Bellamy-Fults representing the Democratic Party, incumbent Jennifer Bradley representing the Republican Party, and Joseph Thornton representing the American Solidarity Party [1, 3, 6]. Because no candidate faced a primary challenger within their respective party, the primary elections scheduled for August 18, 2026, were canceled in accordance with Florida election law, advancing all three candidates directly to the November general election [7, 8, 9, 10]. 

## Candidate Profile: Jason Bellamy-Fults (Democratic)

### Background (Occupation, Education, Prior Public Service)
Jason Bellamy-Fults is a 51-year-old fourth-generation Floridian who grew up in Polk County in a working-class environment, noting in candidate questionnaires that he was raised by a mother who worked as a waitress before opening a small restaurant [1, 7]. He is married to Shay Bellamy-Fults, whom he describes as an educator [1, 11]. His academic credentials begin with a high school diploma from Lakeland High School, followed by a Bachelor of Arts in Biology from Berea College in 2006, where he graduated *Magna Cum Laude* [1, 7, 11]. In 2023, he advanced his education by earning a Master of Arts in Education with a concentration in Educational Technology from the University of Florida, maintaining a 4.0 grade point average [1, 7, 11]. 

Professionally, Bellamy-Fults maintains a multifaceted career spanning academia and skilled labor. He is currently employed in Academic Technology at the University of Florida and serves as the office manager for the United Faculty of Florida at the university [1, 4]. Simultaneously, he is a journeyman wireman who graduated from the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 1205 apprenticeship program, a program to which he subsequently returned as an instructor to train apprentice electricians [1, 4, 11]. Throughout his career, he has also worked as a solar infrastructure installer and an adult educator [4].

His record of public service is rooted in community organizing and municipal advisory roles. He served as the Vice Chair of the Gainesville City Commission's Utility Advisory Board from February 2020 through September 2023 [1]. Additionally, he serves as the Board Chair of the Community Weatherization Coalition and acts as the union liaison for the Alachua County Labor Coalition [1, 4]. Within organized labor, he is the Recording Secretary for IBEW Local 1205, serves as a delegate to the North Central Florida Central Labor Council, and has participated for multiple years in the Florida AFL-CIO Working Family Lobby Corps in Tallahassee [1]. He has not previously held an elected political office [1].

### Stated Positions on Major Issues
According to his campaign website, media questionnaires, and debate statements, Bellamy-Fults’ platform is heavily focused on economic affordability, localized governance, and the expansion of labor rights. On the issue of the economy and cost of living, his campaign emphasizes the need to accept federal tax dollars to expand Medicaid eligibility across Florida, arguing that too many state residents remain uninsured or underinsured [1, 12]. He asserts that all working individuals deserve the right to a livable wage and union representation, tying economic stability to the regulation of public utilities in the interest of ratepayers rather than corporate profits [1, 12].

A central pillar of his campaign is the defense of local control against state preemption. Bellamy-Fults argues that communities should retain the authority to make zoning and development decisions, such as determining whether to permit large-scale developments or data centers in their jurisdictions [11, 12]. He has specifically criticized the current legislature for stripping away rights to local self-governance, including the state's assumption of control over Gainesville Regional Utilities, which he frames as Tallahassee overreach [1, 4].

Regarding environmental policy and natural resources, Bellamy-Fults states that climate change is an impactful reality requiring proactive mitigation strategies. In response to voter guide questionnaires, he recommended restricting the construction of high-rises on barrier islands located in hurricane zones and advocated for a diversified energy portfolio that includes solar, geothermal, and emerging energy-efficiency technologies to better protect the state's freshwater resources [1, 13]. Furthermore, he argues for an end to what he describes as "corporate corruption" in the state capitol, stating that big business lobbyists currently hold disproportionate influence over legislative drafting [12].

### Public Record
Because Bellamy-Fults has not previously held elected office, he lacks a formal legislative voting record [1]. However, his professional and civic record documents substantial involvement in utility regulation and labor advocacy. His tenure on the Gainesville Utility Advisory Board heavily influenced his graduate research, culminating in a master's thesis that evaluated the orientation procedures utilized at public utilities [4]. His campaign materials point to a documented community track record of assisting residents in lowering utility bills, intervening to stop wage theft, and negotiating for improved wages and healthcare access on behalf of local workers [1].

### Campaign Funding
Data from the Florida Division of Elections and independent political trackers covering the 2026 cycle reveal that Bellamy-Fults has run a grassroots-funded campaign. Total receipts for his campaign vary slightly across reporting platforms depending on the specific filing window, with totals ranging between $37,042 and $71,689 [14, 15]. An analysis of his donor demographics indicates that approximately 76% of his contributions originate from individual donors, 20% from entity contributions such as political action committees (PACs), and roughly 4% from self-funding and personal loans [16]. 

His entity-level support is derived entirely from labor organizations and their affiliated advocacy funds, rather than corporate PACs. The top entity contributors to his campaign include the Sheet Metal Workers Local 435 PAC ($2,000), various IBEW PAC Voluntary Funds ($1,000 each), and the Florida Education Association Advocacy Fund ($1,000) [16]. Individual contributions are similarly reflective of his base, with top individual donors including retirees, educators, economists, and local electricians, such as Janice Garry ($1,770) and Anthony D'Agostino ($1,000) [16].

### Publicly Announced Endorsements
Bellamy-Fults has consolidated support among labor unions and progressive organizations throughout the district. His publicly announced endorsements include backing from the Florida AFL-CIO and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) [17, 18]. He has also received endorsements from the National Organization for Women (NOW) and various local and county-level Democratic organizations [17]. In terms of individual political figures, he has secured endorsements from Florida State Senator Brian Nathan and Gainesville City Commissioner James Ingle, both of whom share his affiliation with the IBEW [19]. Conversely, the National Rifle Association-Political Victory Fund assigned Bellamy-Fults a grade of "F" for the 2026 cycle [17].

## Candidate Profile: Jennifer Bradley (Republican, Incumbent)

### Background (Occupation, Education, Prior Public Service)
Jennifer Bradley was born on the Tachikawa U.S. Air Base in Tokyo, Japan [8]. She pursued her undergraduate education at the University of Florida, earning a Bachelor of Science in Criminology in 1991, and subsequently attained a Juris Doctor from the Florida State University College of Law in 1995, where she served on the Law Review [8, 20]. She resides in Clay County with her husband, former Florida State Senator Rob Bradley, with whom she raised three children [20].

Her professional career is rooted in law and commercial property management. Bradley is an attorney who specializes in legal research and drafting, and she previously served as a staff attorney for the judges of Florida's Fourth Judicial Circuit [20, 21]. In the private sector, she is the owner of Hibernia Property Management, Inc., a commercial rental company based in Orange Park, and she acts as the business manager for the law firm of Bradley, Garrison, & Komando, P.A. [8, 20].

Bradley's prior public service is highlighted by her tenure in the Florida State Senate representing District 6. She was first elected in 2020—succeeding her husband in the seat by securing nearly 75% of the general election vote—and assumed office in November 2020 [8, 11, 21]. She subsequently ran unopposed and retained her seat during the 2022 election cycle [4, 8]. Outside of her legislative duties, she has maintained a long-standing civic role as a board member and the founding Board Chair of the PACE Center for Girls in Clay County since 2014, and she is affiliated with the Federated Republican Women of Clay County [2, 20, 21].

### Stated Positions on Major Issues
During the 2026 election cycle, Bradley did not submit responses to standard candidate questionnaires distributed by organizations such as News4JAX, Ballotpedia, and iVoterGuide [1, 8, 22]. As a result, her stated positions must be derived directly from her official campaign literature and her extensive legislative voting record.

Her campaign website frames her platform around the concept of representation aligned with "shared conservative values" [20]. She identifies herself fundamentally as a "Conservative Republican and Business Owner," stating that all 11 counties within her district require a government that listens to their concerns and prioritizes fiscal and social conservatism [20]. Her campaign materials position her as an advocate eager to go to bat for local communities and serve as a representative who fights for the district first [20]. 

### Public Record
As the sitting incumbent, Bradley possesses a highly documented legislative record. During the 2025-2026 legislative term, her leadership roles included serving as the Chair of the Regulated Industries Committee, Vice Chair of the Appropriations Committee on Higher Education, and Alternating Chair of the Joint Committee on Public Counsel Oversight [2, 8]. She also held seats on the Criminal Justice Committee, the Ethics and Elections Committee, and the Senate Rules Committee [8]. Data covering the 2026 regular legislative session indicates that Bradley cast a vote on 98% of the 692 roll calls held, voting in alignment with the Republican majority on 86% of party-line votes [23]. Furthermore, she served as the primary sponsor for five bills that were successfully enacted into law during the session [23].

An analysis of her specific voting record reveals her stances on several pivotal issues. On matters of zoning and housing affordability, she voted in favor of Senate Bill 1080, legislation that standardized zoning application deadlines and imposed limits on the steep escalation of development impact fees [24]. Her environmental and public health record includes voting for Senate Bill 56, which categorized the release of materials into the atmosphere for the purpose of weather modification as a third-degree felony, and Senate Bill 700, a comprehensive agriculture package that protected farmworker housing and ended the mandate for fluoride in public drinking water [24]. In the realm of labor and corporate regulation, Bradley voted for the CHOICE Act (House Bill 1219), a measure permitting high-earning professionals to sign non-compete agreements for durations of up to four years [24]. Notably, on the issue of redistricting, Bradley broke from executive preferences by voting against Governor Ron DeSantis’s mid-decade congressional redistricting map in the Senate Rules Committee, arguing that the proposed map rested on untested legal theories and was "unconstitutional" [21].

### Campaign Funding
Official campaign finance records indicate that Bradley operates with a substantial financial advantage in the District 6 race. Her primary campaign account reported raising $76,791.78 in total contributions during the current cycle [15, 25]. However, this figure is augmented significantly by her control of a separate political committee, named "Women Building the Future," which has reportedly amassed over $2.1 million in available funds [4].

Unlike her challengers, Bradley's top donor categories are heavily populated by corporate entities, industry associations, and institutional political action committees. Her single largest documented contributor is the Florida Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee, Inc., which provided $17,491.78 [25]. Her donor base also includes maximum-level entity contributions from business PACs representing the automotive sector (e.g., Audi West Palm Beach, Braman Imports Inc), the pharmaceutical industry (e.g., Amgen Inc PAC, Eli Lilly and Company), real estate (REALTORS PAC), and regional legal and agricultural firms [4, 25, 26]. 

### Publicly Announced Endorsements
Bradley’s endorsement profile is characterized by robust support from the state's leading business and conservative advocacy organizations. She has secured formal endorsements for the 2026 cycle from the Associated Industries of Florida (AIF), the Florida Chamber of Commerce, and the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) Florida PAC, all of which cited her commitment to free enterprise and economic growth [21, 27, 28]. Additionally, she was endorsed by Florida Right to Life [29]. Scorecard metrics from allied organizations further reflect this support; she holds an 85% conservative excellence rating from the American Conservative Union Foundation and a 70% alignment score from the Republican Liberty Caucus of Florida [2, 22]. 

## Candidate Profile: Joseph Thornton (American Solidarity)

### Background (Occupation, Education, Prior Public Service)
Joseph Thornton is a partially retired academic psychiatrist who has resided in the Gainesville and Alachua County area for more than two decades [30]. He obtained his Bachelor of Arts from the University of Texas at Austin in 1976 and earned a Doctor of Medicine (M.D.) from the University of Texas Health Sciences Center in San Antonio in 1981 [9, 13]. Records also indicate he holds an additional degree or academic credential from Stanford University, completed in 1985 [9]. 

Thornton’s occupational background involves extensive medical practice, institutional leadership, and academic instruction. He spent 15 years as a Clinical Associate Professor with the University of Florida College of Medicine [1, 13]. His medical career also features 12 years of service with the Veterans Administration, where he held the position of Associate Chief of Staff for Mental Health at the North Florida VA [1, 30]. As an educator, he teaches bioethics with a specialized focus on the ethical implications of Artificial Intelligence [30].

His prior public service has primarily been conducted within state and federal institutional healthcare settings. Thornton served in the National Health Service Corps for four years, stationed at the Union Correctional Institution in Raiford [1]. He subsequently spent seven years acting as the Medical Executive Director of a maximum-security forensic treatment facility, identified as the North Florida Evaluation and Treatment Center [1, 30]. In his local community, he founded the Alachua Area Medical Reserve Corps and maintains professional affiliations with the Catholic Medical Association and the Florida Psychiatric Society [9, 13, 31].

### Stated Positions on Major Issues
Thornton's political platform is explicitly guided by the principles of the American Solidarity Party, an organization focused on Christian democratic values, and Catholic social teaching, frequently citing Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical *Magnifica Humanitas* ("Magnificent Humanity") regarding the innate, unearned worth of all human life [1, 32].

A major tenet of his campaign revolves around criminal justice and bioethics. Drawing upon his years of experience providing psychiatric care on death row and consulting in capital cases, Thornton is staunchly opposed to the death penalty, asserting that state violence is not justice [1, 30]. He extends this philosophy to oppose elective abortion, euthanasia, and medically assisted suicide, arguing that human life warrants legal protection from conception until natural death [13]. Furthermore, he advocates for legislation that would strengthen oversight and ensure humane treatment for immigration detainees [1].

Thornton also places significant emphasis on the intersection of technology and labor. He warns against the emerging threats posed by artificial intelligence, arguing that technology must be harnessed to serve human dignity rather than replace it [1, 30]. He asserts that human labor is not a commodity that should be exploited by global economic pressures or algorithmic subjugation [1]. 

Economically, Thornton aligns with the concept of "distributism"—a philosophy that supports private property rights but seeks to actively defend society against oligarchic wealth concentration and government overreach [13]. He prioritizes the elimination of government waste by ending the practice of utilizing public resources to protect corporate profits and calls for heightened transparency in state decision-making [13]. On matters of election integrity, he supports systemic reforms such as implementing ranked-choice voting, opening primary elections, establishing term limits, and curbing corporate campaign financing [1]. He has also voiced opposition to strict photo identification laws for voting if such requirements impose an unfair hardship on citizens [13].

### Public Record
As a first-time candidate, Thornton does not possess a legislative voting record [1]. His documented professional record is anchored in his decades of medical administration, where his stated focus has been on protecting vulnerable populations, reducing institutional violence, and promoting dignity among veterans, individuals with severe mental illness, and incarcerated persons [30]. In his capacity as a private citizen and bioethics advocate, he has drafted proposed legislative frameworks aimed at abolishing the death penalty in Florida and instituting oversight protocols for facilities housing immigration detainees [1, 30].

### Campaign Funding
An examination of campaign finance filings demonstrates that Thornton's campaign operates on a micro-budget structure, entirely independent of corporate or institutional backing. Official reports indicate total contributions of $5,177.66 for the 2026 cycle [15]. This total is comprised of individual donor contributions and personal self-funding, which includes documented personal loans amounting to $577 [15]. The campaign has reported zero income from political action committees or official party committees [15].

### Publicly Announced Endorsements
According to a comprehensive review of independent election trackers and provided research materials, Joseph Thornton has not received any publicly announced endorsements from third-party political action committees, elected officials, or prominent advocacy groups outside of the structural backing of his own American Solidarity Party [31, 33]. 

---

## Comparative Campaign Finance Dynamics





The campaign finance architecture of the District 6 race highlights stark differences in candidate viability models. The financial dominance of the incumbent, Jennifer Bradley, relies heavily on the aggregation of resources from corporate PACs, industry groups, and the formal Republican party apparatus, a mechanism that has allowed her to stockpile over $2 million across multiple accounts [4, 25]. This war chest is indicative of the structural benefits of incumbency in an ideologically safe district. Conversely, the challengers rely on divergent, grassroots models. Bellamy-Fults' funding relies on high individual donor density combined with strategic, small-dollar injections from specialized labor PACs, tying his financial health directly to union organizing [16]. Thornton’s entirely self-funded and micro-donor model highlights the profound financial barriers third-party candidates face in establishing competitive infrastructure without institutional backing [15].
